title: Processes, threads and signals
description: Understand Linux processes and threads as the building blocks of every production system.

data.text: In production Linux systems, almost every issue leads back to processes and threads. A process is an instance of a running program. Each process has its own memory space, file descriptors, and environment. A thread is a lighter unit that runs inside a process and shares memory with other threads in the same process.

When something goes wrong on a server, your first questions are usually: What is running? Which process is using the most CPU? Is it stuck? Why did it exit? Signals are one of the primary ways Linux communicates with processes. Understanding how processes, threads, and signals interact is essential for diagnosing production issues.

Every program you start on Linux becomes a process. The kernel assigns each process a unique ID called a PID (Process ID). When you run a command, you can see its PID using commands like ps or top. A process contains the program code, its current activity, a stack, heap, data section, and file descriptors.

Processes can create child processes using the fork system call. The parent process can wait for the child to finish. In web applications, a master process often spawns worker processes to handle requests. If a worker crashes, the master can restart it.

items: PID (Process ID): unique number for each running process
PPID (Parent Process ID): identifies which process started this one
UID/GID: user and group that own the process
State: running, sleeping, stopped, or zombie

data.text: A thread is the smallest unit of execution within a process. A single process can contain multiple threads. Threads share the same memory space but each has its own stack and program counter. Multi-threaded applications, like web servers, use threads to handle multiple connections at once.

Threads are faster to create than processes because they share memory. However, they require careful synchronization because two threads writing to the same memory can corrupt data. When troubleshooting, knowing whether an application is multi-threaded helps you interpret CPU and memory usage correctly.
Signals: how Linux talks to processes

A signal is a notification sent to a process to tell it that an event has occurred. Signals can come from the kernel, from another process, or from the process itself. Each signal has a number and a default action: terminate, stop, continue, or ignore.

When you press Ctrl+C, you send SIGINT. When a process runs out of memory, the kernel may send SIGKILL. When you stop a process with kill, you usually send SIGTERM first to give it time to clean up. SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored, so it is the last resort.

The ps command shows a snapshot of running processes. The top command provides a live updating view. Both are essential for troubleshooting. You can filter ps output to find specific processes, and you can sort top by CPU or memory usage.

data.code:
ps aux | grep nginx
top -p 1234
kill -SIGTERM 1234
kill -0 1234   # check if process exists

data.title: Watch out for zombies
data.text: A zombie process is a child that has finished executing but still has an entry in the process table because its parent has not yet read its exit status. Zombies do not use CPU or memory, but they do use a process ID. A large number of zombies can prevent new processes from starting.

items: A web server is not responding: check if the process is running, check its state, check CPU and memory usage
A deployment failed: check if the old process was sent SIGTERM and whether it exited cleanly
High CPU: identify the process with top or ps, then check if it is stuck in a loop or doing legitimate work
Out of memory: check which process is using the most memory, check for memory leaks

data.title: Key Takeaways
items: Every running program is a process with a unique PID
Threads run inside processes and share memory
Signals are lightweight messages that tell a process to do something
Always use SIGTERM before SIGKILL to allow graceful shutdown
Zombie processes mean the parent is not cleaning up children properly
